canberra.title: Canberra’s overnight nursing service under review but closure’s off the table
canberra.snippet: An overnight nursing service that provides critical support to seriously ill Canberrans in their homes is facing proposed changes, raisin...
canberra.content:
Canberra’s overnight LINK nursing service provides vital support to palliative care patients receiving treatment at home. Photo: File.

An overnight nursing service that provides critical support to seriously ill Canberrans in their homes is facing proposed changes, raising concerns about whether patients receiving palliative care and other treatments will continue to have access to nurses after hours.

Canberra Health Services (CHS) has confirmed a formal consultation is underway on changes to the LINK Nursing service, but insists the proposal does not involve closing it.

Patients can contact trained nurses for assistance, and staff can arrange home visits after assessing their needs and consulting specialists where necessary.

In response to questions from Region, a CHS spokesperson said a consultation paper had been distributed seeking feedback on proposed changes to the service.

“The proposal does not involve closure of the LINK service. No decisions have been made at this time, with consultation currently underway,” the spokesperson said.

“The consultation process and the feedback received will all be considered before the service model is finalised by Canberra Health Services.”

Consultation began on 6 November and involves CHS staff and several organisations, including ACT Ambulance Service, Carers ACT, the Health Care Consumers Association of the ACT and Palliative Care ACT.

However, CHS has not detailed what specific changes are being proposed or whether overnight home visits, staffing arrangements or the range of patients supported could be affected.

The uncertainty comes as questions are raised about the sustainability of round-the-clock nursing care for patients who are too unwell to attend hospital or are receiving end-of-life care at home.

During a recent hearing, CHS palliative care director Michael Chapman acknowledged difficulties maintaining the service.

Dr Chapman said LINK played an important role in ensuring patients receiving specialist palliative care at home could access professional support overnight.

“If a person has issues and is a patient of this home-based palliative care service with specialist palliative care needs, and they call to get support, they’re speaking to a nurse from the LINK service,” he said.

The nurse then consults specialists on call to determine whether the patient needs an in-person visit.

Dr Chapman said the review was intended to establish whether the current arrangements were the most effective and sustainable way of providing 24-hour support.

“There have been challenges, I understand, in maintaining this service through LINK, and there is a consultation process that’s recently been kicked off to try and determine whether this is the most effective and sustainable way of continuing that 24/7 support for community patients who need palliative care support,” he said.

The prospect of changes has prompted concern among people familiar with the service. In an online discussion, one contributor described LINK as an integral part of Canberra’s health system, saying its nurses provided overnight assistance to patients undergoing chemotherapy and those needing catheter care, wound care and other urgent nursing attention.

The contributor warned that losing overnight support could have serious consequences for people receiving palliative care at home.

“It would be a disaster to not have this service,” the commenter wrote.

Another contributor said she had referred numerous patients to LINK over the years.

“Have never used it myself but have referred many patients to the service,” she wrote.

“Would be a huge loss for Canberrans to lose this service.”

While CHS has ruled out closure under the current proposal, it has not explained whether the existing level of overnight nursing support would be maintained. However, it said feedback from staff and stakeholders would be considered before a final decision was made.

It has not said when the consultation will conclude or when the proposed service model will be finalised.

canberra.title: Fruit picker’s catastrophic ladder fall sparks $1.9m legal battle between states
canberra.snippet: A fruit picker left paralysed after falling from a ladder at a Hillston orchard has become the centre of a $1.9 million legal battle betw...
canberra.content:
Ching Tam fell off a ladder while picking tangelos. Photo: PxHere/file.

A fruit picker left paralysed after falling from a ladder at a Hillston orchard has become the centre of a $1.9 million legal battle between NSW and Victorian workers compensation authorities.

The NSW Court of Appeal has ruled Victoria must reimburse iCare $1.915 million after the NSW insurer mistakenly paid benefits to the injured worker over several years.

According to published court judgments, the worker, Ching Tam, suffered catastrophic spinal injuries in the accident on 13 July 2017, leaving him a quadriplegic with a total loss of movement in his arms and legs.

The Malaysian citizen fell from a long ladder while picking tangelos at an orchard operated by Super Seasons Pty Ltd at Hillston, but was employed through a Melbourne-based labour hire company, Mr Handy Professor Pty Ltd.

Before arriving in Hillston, Mr Tam had worked as a fruit picker in Shepparton in Victoria.

That employment history became central to a dispute over which states’ workers compensation scheme was responsible for supporting him.

“Although the location of the accident was obvious, uncertainty arose with respect to the question of who was responsible for Mr Tam’s undisputed entitlement to workers compensation payments and benefits,” a judgment handed down last week stated.

“This uncertainty arose from the fact that Mr Tam’s employer was based in Victoria and the fact that he had usually worked for that employer in that state.”

Under cross-border workers compensation rules, a claim is generally handled by the state where a worker usually works for their employer, rather than necessarily where they are injured.

Although Mr Tam was injured in NSW, his employment was connected to Victoria. However, Victoria’s WorkCover authority initially rejected his claim, arguing it was a NSW matter.

Mr Handy Professor was uninsured in NSW, so iCare initially accepted liability and began paying compensation to Mr Tam or on his behalf. Super Seasons could potentially have been held responsible as the principal contractor under NSW law.

Victoria eventually accepted liability in August 2022 after his Victorian employment connection was confirmed. By then, iCare had already paid more than $1.5 million in benefits.

The dispute between the two insurers emerged from broader NSW Supreme Court proceedings in which Mr Tam sued orchard operator Super Seasons Pty Ltd and both state authorities over his injuries.

Those personal injury proceedings were discontinued in July 2024, leaving iCare’s separate claim against Victoria as the remaining dispute.

Although Mr Tam was also named as a second defendant to iCare’s claim as the person who received the benefit of the funds, iCare eventually abandoned any claim to recover the compensation from him personally.

Victoria accepted it was responsible for the worker’s compensation but argued it should not have to reimburse NSW because it had not directly received the money.

After losing in the NSW Supreme Court last year, where a judge ordered it to pay $1,915,218.43, Victoria took the matter to the Court of Appeal.

The NSW Court of Appeal ruled by a 2-1 majority that Victoria had benefited because iCare’s mistaken payments discharged a legal debt Victoria was otherwise required to pay the injured worker.

The court found this amounted to “unjust enrichment” under restitution law, even though no money had gone directly to the Victorian authority.

The court dismissed Victoria’s appeal and upheld the order requiring it to pay the $1.915 million, as well as iCare’s legal costs.

One judge disagreed, finding Victoria had not received a benefit from iCare’s payments and should not have to reimburse it. He also argued iCare had an alternative legal avenue to recover the money from Mr Tam, which it had chosen not to pursue.

The ruling does not require Mr Tam to repay the compensation, with the financial battle strictly between the two state authorities.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Dodgy tradie stole $100,000 from more than 25 victims
canberra.snippet: Over about two years, a dodgy tradesman scammed numerous Canberrans out of nearly $100,000 by promising to complete works at their homes ...
canberra.content:
25 November 2026

Shawn John Michelin arrives at the City Police Station after his arrest in November 2025. Photo: ACT Policing.

Over about two years, a dodgy tradesman scammed numerous Canberrans out of nearly $100,000 by promising to complete works at their homes that he never finished.

Shawn John Michelin continued to defraud his victims even after learning he was being investigated by ACT Fair Trading, which issued a public warning about him.

He wouldn’t or couldn’t stop, and his activities were only brought to an end when he was arrested and charged last November.

The 27-year-old spent about a year in custody before appearing in the ACT Magistrates Court on Wednesday (25 November), where he was convicted and sentenced to a total of three years and seven months in jail.

Magistrate Ian Temby said between July 2023 and November 2025, Michelin advertised construction and landscaping services on Facebook.

The magistrate said he visited potential customers in person to gain their trust, gave them written quotes and obtained deposits to do work at their properties. But he didn’t complete the work and in some cases never even started it.

Michelin used fake names for himself and regularly changed his business name.

He used phones registered to members of his family to contact victims, and on one occasion he impersonated the real business of a family member.

In total, he performed his scheme 25 times on singles or couples in Canberra, defrauding them of $96,584.

Magistrate Temby said each victim suffered financial losses and inconvenience.

One victim said the $500 Michelin stole represented a week’s wages, while a couple said they had been preparing to get married and the financial consequences of his crime meant they had been unable to take a honeymoon.

The magistrate said it was not a particularly sophisticated scheme. But he also noted Michelin falsely claimed he would complete the works or promised refunds in attempts to get more money from his victims or to delay them from making complaints about him.

Prosecutors told the court there was no evidence Michelin was even qualified to perform the works he agreed to undertake. But the magistrate said he didn’t know what qualifications would be required.

He also accepted that Michelin at least partly defrauded his victims to fund his drug habit.

Michelin pleaded guilty to 25 counts of obtaining property by deception, as well as to unrelated charges.

He asked for an intensive corrections order, which is a type of community-based sentence, to complete a residential drug rehabilitation course.

But Magistrate Temby said this would not be appropriate, partly due to the seriousness of his offending, the fact he harmed many members of the community and the risk of him reoffending.

He was handed a non-parole period of two years’ jail, which means he can be released from custody in November 2027 due to time served.

He was also ordered to pay compensation to the victims of his fraud.

The courtroom was packed on Wednesday, and Michelin stared intently at Magistrate Temby while he was being sentenced.

canberra.title: Inflation hits 4.9 per cent, leaving government in damage control
canberra.snippet: Inflation jumped to 4.9 per cent in the year to October, up from 4.3 per cent in September and fuelling fears of an imminent recession. A...
canberra.content:
The cost-of-living crisis continues, with inflation reaching 4.9 per cent. Photo: Envato Elements.

Inflation jumped to 4.9 per cent in the year to October, up from 4.3 per cent in September and fuelling fears of an imminent recession.

Annual underlying inflation lifted from 3.6 per cent in September to 3.8 per cent in October.

Labor is playing down the prospects of a recession – with a technical recession requiring six months of negative real gross domestic product (GDP) growth.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics are an “unwelcome but unsurprising” reminder of the pressure Australians are under.

“October saw inflation rise in most major advanced economies and interest rates are going up around the world as a result,” he said.

“Since September, every major advanced economy has had a rate rise, and the market is pricing further rate hikes in every one of them.

“Inflation is still much lower than its peak in 2022, but it’s still too high.

“We had an inflation challenge in our economy before the conflict in the Middle East, but the war is making it worse.

“This inflation challenge is the primary influence on the budget update we will finalise in the coming weeks and release in December.”

The Treasurer said the inflation challenge was the primary influence on next month’s budget update, which is still being finalised.

He said the Federal Government will respond this week with “substantial savings” and additional cost-of-living help.

“The budget is not the primary driver of prices in our economy, but we take our responsibilities in the fight against inflation seriously, and that’s a major focus of next month’s MYEFO,” Dr Chalmers said.

But shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said the cost-of-living crisis many Australians are facing was Labor’s doing.

“The Treasurer’s job is to defeat inflation and get costs down for families and small businesses, but inflation has defeated the Treasurer in the economy Labor built,” Mr Wilson said.

“Higher inflation is not a bug of the economy Labor built, it is a design feature, and Australians face the risk of another interest rate rise, and paying more at the supermarket, and getting less.

“The latest inflation data today is another devastating blow to Australia’s economy.

“Australia’s inflation crisis started in July 2025, seven months before a single bomb was dropped on Tehran.

“Inflation has remained consistently high, above the RBA’s target band since then. And as the RBA has said, international factors have compounded the inflation problem that already existed within the domestic economy.”

The Australian Council of Trade Unions is urging the Reserve Bank not to raise interest rates despite the latest inflation figures.

ACTU secretary Melissa Donnelly said the new inflation figures, alongside the latest employment data [unemployment has hit 4.9 per cent], confirm that working Australians are doing it tough.

“Unions are calling on the Reserve Bank to resist the temptation to increase interest rates when it meets next month,” she said.

“Working people can’t afford more financial stress, especially at a time when their jobs are increasingly at risk, and higher rates will do nothing to fix the structural problems in the economy.

“Corporate Australia should use its mega profits to absorb a greater share of overseas cost pressures instead of passing it on to Australian families.

“Companies decide what prices to charge, and they can choose to prioritise people’s livelihoods over protecting their profits.”

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive officer Andrew McKellar described the inflation figure as an “alarming result” for Australia.

“It shows that there’s still significant inflation pressure in the economy. It’s a bad sign for business, and I think it should ring alarm bells with government that we do need urgent action,” he said.

“We need to address the challenges to lift the speed limits and capacity in the economy.

“Clearly, we don’t want to see the risk that there could be further interest rate increases ahead.

“We absolutely need to do more to take the pressure off the economy, off business, off small business at this time.”

ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck said housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in October, rising 6.4 per cent compared to 5.2 per cent in the 12 months to September.

Electricity rose 25.2 per cent in the 12 months to October, up from 12.8 per cent in the 12 months to September.

New dwelling prices rose 5.1 per cent in the 12 months to October, up from 4.7 per cent to September. This was driven by builders passing on higher material and labour costs.

“The 6.4 per cent rise in annual inflation for housing reflected increases for both electricity and new dwellings expenditure classes,” Ms McCririck said.

“The rise in electricity reflects Commonwealth government rebates, which reduced household electricity costs last year but are no longer in place.”

Transport was the second largest contributor to annual inflation in October, rising by 10.6 per cent due to higher automotive fuel prices.

“On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 6.3 per cent in October, compared to a rise of 9.4 per cent in September. This was driven by higher world oil prices,” Ms McCririck said.

canberra.title: Ex-top rugby player jailed for raping woman inside her own home
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence. A former top rugby player decided to go to a woman’s home in Canberra unin...
canberra.content:
Paula Fala Kata, 38, has been sentenced to 2.5 years in jail.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence.

A former top rugby player decided to go to a woman’s home in Canberra uninvited, then begged her to kiss him before he raped her in her doorway.

Paula Fala Kata, a 38-year-old who used to play in Tonga’s national rugby team, has now been sentenced to 2.5 years’ jail over his repulsive assault.

The ACT Supreme Court heard he met the woman sometime before they began messaging each other in 2024. He sent her messages like, “Maybe one day I stop by and say hi”, and “I want to see you”.

“Lol, no you are not single,” she replied on one occasion, before eventually blocking him. This prevented him from sending her messages again.

But the court heard Kata then went to her home uninvited and unexpectedly in June 2024, arriving early on a Sunday morning.

The woman had been asleep and woke up to the sound of her gate opening and footsteps outside. She met him at the door and asked him what he was doing, but he didn’t give her a clear answer.

She let him come inside to speak with her but told him he wasn’t supposed to be there and that he wouldn’t see her again.

Kata pleaded with her to kiss him, suggested they have sex, kissed her without permission and digitally raped her. This occurred while the woman told him “no” and tried to push him away.

She managed to push him out of her home, then went to the police later that day.

The court heard Kata fought the charges against him at a jury trial, but jurors ultimately found him guilty of sexual intercourse without consent and committing an act of indecency without consent.

At his sentencing on Wednesday (25 November), Justice Belinda Baker said the woman had told the court she could not fathom going from being at home, slowly waking up to a Sunday morning, to now facing struggles every day.

The woman also told the court she felt she just had to accept some events affected people so much they may never be the same, just beautifully different.

“It hurts, it really hurts,” the woman said.

“My journey does not end here … My road to healing and recovery continues for a long time.”

Justice Baker said Kata claimed he thought the woman had been consenting and he later suggested she may have been lying to obtain victims of crime compensation. However, the judge said his version was rejected by the jury at his trial, and she was satisfied about the woman’s credibility.

“The offender’s actions violated the victim’s bodily integrity,” she said.

“Once he entered the victim’s home, he ignored her physical and verbal protests.”

Kata had a positive upbringing and was a professional footballer from 2007 to 2018, until an injury ended his sporting career.

He had a supportive partner, stable employment in the construction industry and no prior convictions.

His sentence was backdated by 13 days to account for time spent in custody. He was also given a 15-month non-parole period, which means he can be released from jail in February 2028.

Kata gave no visible reaction to his sentence when he was led off into custody.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

australia.title: Australia’s most progressive state is poised to turn blue. How would Victoria change under a Coalition government?
australia.snippet: Jess Wilson says the Liberal and National parties will implement policies to ‘fix’ Victoria if they win the state election. Here’s what’s...
australia.content:
Victoria is on the cusp of a political transformation. After 12 years of Labor rule, the state long regarded as Australia’s most progressive is poised to turn blue, and, in turn, challenge the way Victorians see themselves.

“That self-image that was important in the Andrews era of being ‘the Massachusetts of Australia’, a notably progressive sort of state, is going to take a battering,” Frank Bongiorno, an Australian historian at the University of Canberra, says.

With just days left until the state election, the Liberal-National Coalition has run a small-target campaign under its leader, Jess Wilson, determined to keep the focus on an unpopular Labor government. But its policy ambition is clear in public documents – even if voters are more focused on sending a message to Labor.

“Many will breathe in, or grit their teeth, and vote Coalition,” Bongiorno says. “It is an anti-government, anti-Labor vote and I think that suggests a certain shallowness in terms of the support for the other side.”

While this protest vote will decide the election, Bongiorno says it may also deliver a fragile mandate that could be “a drain on what a Coalition government can actually get away with in office”.

“They’re going to have to earn it. It’s going to be very difficult.”

The first 100 days

The Coalition has made its short-term priorities clear.

By March next year, if it takes government, it will have repealed Australia’s first formal treaty with First Nations people, introduced harsher bail laws and tougher sentences for children, clamped down on protest, opened up new gas exploration, scrapped a major renewable energy transmission project and reversed a ban on gas in new homes.

It will have expanded the royal commission into allegations of corruption on government construction sites and cut several taxes, alongside Labor’s planning provisions that allowed for more development near 60 train and tram stations across Melbourne.

In recent weeks, it has also announced plans to recriminalise begging, review the use of puberty blockers and relocate a medically supervised safe injecting facility in North Richmond.

Wilson has framed these policies as “disciplined decisions” to “fix” Victoria. But many have strident critics who argue they unwind progressive policies that, in some cases, took more than a decade to negotiate.

The Liberal plan to repeal Victoria’s treaty has featured heavily in messaging from Labor and Greens candidates in progressive seats. The Coalition says the treaty, which gives First Nations people a greater say in laws that affect their lives, is divisive and expensive.

Djaran Murray-Jackson is the co-chair of Victoria’s First People’s Assembly, established as part of the treaty process. He says the treaty must “remain above party politics if we are truly going to deliver practical change for our people’s lives”.

First Nations leaders have also raised concerns about the Coalition’s youth sentencing policy, inspired by the Queensland Liberal National government. The so-called “adult crime, adult time” plan would allow children to be sentenced as adults for 20 serious offences and would be legislated before Christmas, alongside a new one-strike rule for bail.

Nerita Waight, the chief executive of the Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service, says the two proposals would add further pressure to police cells and prisons already at capacity.

“We are incredibly concerned that any more strain on the system makes a death in custody inevitable,” Waight says.

The Coalition also plans to reinstate “move-on laws” for protesters by March and beyond that, a permit system for demonstrations and a ban on the phrase “globalise the intifada”. This is despite a similar ban, also introduced by the Queensland government, facing a high court challenge.

Gemma Cafarella, the president of civil rights organisation Liberty Victoria, expects any attempt to introduce similar legislation in the state to face a legal challenge.

“If the Coalition follows through on these commitments, people are going to have to fight for their human rights and civil liberties,” she says.

While the Coalition has no plans to reverse Victoria’s emission reduction targets – cutting greenhouse gas emissions by between 75% to 80% below 2005 levels by 2035, and reaching net zero emissions by 2045 – it will rip up policies that were in part designed to reduce carbon emissions.

The Coalition would overturn a long-standing ban on gas exploration, cancel a proposed transmission line to New South Wales that would support renewable energy integration and cancel plans to phase out gas in new homes.

Alison Reeve, of the Grattan Institute, says reversing bans on domestic gas could make a shortage worse and that any new gas reserves would take at leave five years to come online. Ultimately, she says some of these promises may need to be broken.

“The alternative is that the next energy minister will be fronting the cameras in 2028 explaining why the lights are flickering,” she says.

The long-term challenge

Wilson knows one of her toughest challenge will be the state’s finances, as debt soars and the economy slows.

While Labor spruiks an operating surplus, this figure doesn’t include infrastructure or other capital spending. When factored in, Victoria remains cash deficit in the billions over the forward estimates.

Victoria’s debt also continues to grow, projected to hit almost $200bn in 2029-30 – the highest of all state and territory governments. By then, interest payments on state debt are forecast to total $11.82bn – or $32m a day.

The Liberals have released a 10-year economic plan which includes a goal of returning to a cash surplus by 2032. To do this, they need to find about $30bn in savings. They have so far identified $26bn, largely through a proposed decade-long hiring freeze on public service jobs.

At the same time, the party has made more than $8.6bn in election commitments, according to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), as well as up to $5bn worth of tax cuts it plans to legislate in the first parliament sitting.

Ahead of the PBO’s release of its costings of the Liberal and National parties’ policies on Thursday, the Coalition said its plan would see the state’s net debt fall by more than 10% over the forward estimates – hitting $176bn in 2029-30 rather than $196bn under Labor.

The plan has prompted skepticism from some economists, including David Hayward and Saul Eslake, while an analysis by the progressive think tank the Australian Institute estimates almost 32,000 public service jobs would need to go to deliver the promised $22bn in savings.

Others, including members of the Economic Society of Australia, are calling for a more aggressive approach to bring the state’s spending down. Zac Gross, a senior economics lecturer at Monash University, agrees.

He says the Coalition may need to reconsider “obviously popular” policies such as a $50 weekly toll cap and make difficult decisions about the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop, which he calls the “elephant in the room”.

The Coalition has committed to “pause and review” SRL East, 26km of tunnels that make up the first stage of the rail project, though Labor has already signed more than $14.5bn in construction contracts that may be difficult to break.

The public service is also bracing for major structural changes, including senior appointments to government departments, agencies and boards after 12 years of Labor. Work has already begun, with a trio of MPs retiring at the election – former Liberal leader Michael O’Brien, former Nationals leader Peter Walsh and Kim Wells – tapped to lead Wilson’s transition team.

In the final days of the election campaign, Bongiorno has a warning to Liberals who may be thinking about 1992, when Liberal leader Jeff Kennett ended a decade of Labor rule.

“It seemed to some observers that Victoria was reverting to its traditional political pattern,” says Bongiorno, referencing the party’s historical power base in Victoria, the home to its founder Robert Menzies.

“That turned out to be a complete misreading of the patterns of Victorian politics because Labor has really dominated since – with Kennett as a kind of interlude.”

australia.title: Aidan is one of thousands of students forced to verbally defend his honours thesis as universities take on AI
australia.snippet: Honours students are increasingly being asked to sit oral assessments – but at the University of Sydney it’s become a requirement for all...
australia.content:
When Aidan Elwig Pollock signed up for an honours program at the University of Sydney, he did not expect his 20,000-word thesis to be accompanied by a spoken component.

But, as AI increasingly makes written research an unreliable form of assessment, the university has demanded all students taking the one-year program defend their arguments in conversation with professors.

Top Australian universities are increasingly asking honours students to sit oral assessments, with Sydney the first known to require it across honours programs.

Exams have moved from computers back to paper or interviews in the four years since the release of ChatGPT made AI plagiarism a concern. Some educators have adopted the debate-focused tutorials traditional at Oxbridge colleges or the viva voce assessments typical of PhDs.

But honours programs – a year of intensive research for dedicated students after their bachelor’s degree – have been slower to adapt as they’re typically focused on a single project, which accounts for most of their grade.

Elwig Pollock, a history student, said he had not used AI at all on his work on how the commemoration of Captain Cook has evolved over time, and that the new demand was “insulting” to students and the professors who supervise them.

“If you’ve used AI to do your honours thesis and your supervisor has not figured it out throughout your regular meetings, then what’s stopping you from communicating that material successfully in a 15-minute conversation,” Elwig Pollock said.

Since 2024, Sydney bachelor’s degrees have included a mix of assessments that are vulnerable or secure to AI tools. This year, the university has formally extended that to honours programs, though the format is different for every faculty.

On Wednesday, Elwig Pollock had a short conversation which was a pass or fail hurdle task but was worth nothing towards his final grade. In his case most of his marks are coming from his thesis but his degree will not be awarded if he fails the conversation.

Engineering student Isabelle* had an entirely different experience.

Last week, the University of Sydney student had an hour of interviews with professors in a single room with five classmates, as the school rushed through assessing 250 students in two days. It accounted for 50% of her grade.

Her 20,000-word thesis was worth just 20%.

“There were people coming in and out of the room while we were being assessed so it was distracting,” said Isabelle, who asked for a pseudonym to avoid being penalised.

“[We had to] move to the other side of the room so my marker could hear me.”

The change has stressed students who aren’t used to speaking up in class, don’t speak English as a first language or need their honours to become qualified in their field – including engineers like Isabelle.

“I think it’s particularly bad in engineering because writing skills are poor, but I think it’s a Band-Aid solution,” she said of the verbal component.

Adam Bridgeman, the university’s acting deputy vice-chancellor for education, said honours degrees needed to change.

“We necessarily treat honours theses as open assessments as we can’t reliably restrict AI use,” Bridgeman said.

Staff and students were offered guidance and practice to manage the transformation and ensure English fluency and speaking ability were not “inadvertently rewarded”, he said.

“We appreciate some students might be nervous about the experience, especially if it’s their first time,” Bridgeman said. “We’ll take feedback on board as we plan for 2027 assessments.”

While Sydney is the only major institution to mandate interviews for honours programs, schools at the University of Melbourne, Monash University and Australian Catholic University are bringing them in.

Adelaide University, which was previously among the first in Australia to reintroduce viva voce tasks, is using “interactive oral assessments” in which students and teachers role-play real-world professional situations.

There are no public reports of Australian honours students cheating with AI. Kurt Iveson, an honours coordinator for Sydney’s School of Geosciences, said the change was still needed to respond to AI’s growing role in education.

“They’re not the kind of people that I would personally be worried about getting Claude to write their honours thesis for them,” Iveson said.

“But … [management] want to be able to demonstrate to the world, as part of their social licence and external accreditation, that things are being assessed securely.”

The interviews are a heavy addition to professors’ workloads – and no casuals have been brought on to help. Staff and students contacted by Guardian Australia said the new rules had left supervisors feeling rushed and overworked.

But, Iveson said, interviews are a valuable way of helping students learn and understand the significance of their research.

“Assuming that you have actually written it, you know your shit, you’ll be fine, and you’ll have a good conversation.”

*Name has been changed

australia.title: Hundreds of applications and no offers: the young Australians looking for work as economy hits perfect storm
australia.snippet: As unemployment and inflation rise, many young Australians are feeling anxious and ‘defeated’ amid the struggle to find secure jobs Get o...
australia.content:
For Imogen, it’s been a tough year. She’s applied for more than 200 jobs, interviewed for about 20 and landed none.

The 21-year-old lost her job at a large supermarket chain last September after she started having severe pain, likely endometriosis, and dropped back to casual work. Within three months, she was taken off the roster.

“They’re like, don’t come back until you figure out what’s going on,” Imogen says. “That was hard because I had just moved out of home for the first time and I was living with a housemate … that’s what led me to apply for Centrelink.”

Imogen is one of the 753,700 Australians who are struggling to find work – a number that continues to rise.

On Wednesday, inflation hit 4.9% in the year to October, sparking fears of a recession as cost-of-living pressures peak. It came after the Rental Affordability Index, which measures rental costs relative to incomes, revealed on Tuesday that median rents in much of the country now eat up between 30% and 33% of household incomes.

It’s a perfect storm, and some economists are warning it could cause long-running problems for young people trying to get a job.

Imogen lives in a share house in the Hunter Valley in New South Wales. She shops at foodbanks where possible, compares supermarket prices before she purchases and hardly goes out; the rare times she agrees to meeting friends out, she will order the cheapest thing on the menu. She loves swing dancing, but has had to mostly say no to performing at events because of the cost associated.

She worked at a local takeaway shop and McDonald’s before entering customer service at the supermarket for three years. She has six years of experience in the workforce – but can’t get a job.

“Every time I go for an interview and I get the response that actually, no, we’re not interested, I feel so defeated,” she says. “It’s affected my mental health. I’ve got the qualifications, I’ve got a good connection with customers, I’ve got everything I need for a job. Why won’t anyone just hire me?”

Unemployment jumped to 4.9% in October, and younger Australians, aged between 15 and 24, are being the hardest hit. Youth unemployment hit 11.3% – the highest it’s been since October 2021. Since Covid, or May 2022, the youth unemployment rate has averaged 9.2%.

‘They’ll be stigmatised in the future’

Richard Denniss, the co-chief executive of the Australia Institute, says young people are disproportionately affected because when employers get nervous they stop filling new roles and shed casual workers – roles often taken up by younger Australians.

What’s happening now could have deleterious consequences on young people looking for work, with some spending extended periods of time out of work, Denniss says.

“In Australia we still stigmatise unemployment very heavily and brutally,” he says. “That means that the people who are becoming unemployed because of our fight against inflation, those people will not only be asked to live below the poverty line, but they’ll be stigmatised in the future for their experience.”

Another driver of the high youth unemployment is that there are more young people in the job market than there have been in the past 50 years, says Blair Chapman, the chief economist at Seek.

“More people are looking for second jobs to help supplement their incomes due to rising living costs,” he says. “This means that younger workers are not only competing with other unemployed people for work, but they are also competing with some employed people who are looking to boost their hours and incomes with second jobs.”

The number of jobs added on Seek is falling, down 6.4% in the year, while the number of applications per ad has risen for eight consecutive months.

Josh, 28, knows this too well. He’s spent years working as a journalist before moving into the public service in NSW. He took some time off to live in Paris, before relocating to Melbourne and is now struggling to get back into employment.

Since May, he’s applied for 107 jobs – mostly for the Victorian government and local councils. He’s had one interview and two assessment tasks and heard nothing. He says most roles he’s applying for on LinkedIn have more than 100 applications.

“I focused a lot on trying to find a job in the Victorian government,” he says. “Which I think is futile, especially with the election looming and the possibilities of a hiring freeze post-election.”

With no other options, Josh is about to start a master of public health and will apply for hospitality jobs to keep him afloat while he studies.

“The idea is that, ideally, by the end of that degree, my employability would be higher slash unemployment would be lower,” he says.

“In other economic settings … I think I would have a job by now.”

The independent economist Saul Eslake says in the short term there is no magic switch to flick that will help people find employment.

“There’s nothing that can be done in a short period of time,” Eslake says. “If there was anything governments or companies could do to lift productivity so that the economy can produce more goods and services that people want to buy without putting upward pressure on prices, that would help.

“But again, that’s not something that can be done [quickly] and seeing the result in six to twelve weeks.”

If you’re unemployed right now, it’s going to be tricky to find a job in the next 12 months without reinventing yourself – moving to areas where unemployment is lower, or getting a new skill.

“It is quite plausible that we could have a year or two of the unemployment rate being north of five,” Eslake says.

australia.title: Large bushfire threatens homes and properties on Flinders Island off Tasmania
australia.snippet: Blaze spreads significantly across the north of Flinders Island after being started by lightning strikes Get our breaking news email , fr...
australia.content:
Homes and properties on a picturesque remote island were under threat on Wednesday night from an out-of-control bushfire that had sent smoke hundreds of kilometres south.

The blaze on Flinders Island in Bass Strait spread significantly on Wednesday after being started by lightning strikes.

As of Wednesday night, six emergency warnings were in place, including for the coastal settlement of Killiecrankie and nearby areas Leeka, Mount Tanner, Mount Boyes and Carnacs Flat.

Just before 9pm, the Tasmania fire Sservice warned that an uncontained bushfire at Palana was travelling towards Leeka and Mount Tanner.

The agency said conditions had moderated but people who were not prepared should be ready to leave for a safer place.

Some structures had been destroyed but it was too early to tell whether they were homes, the Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said.

The Tasmanian premier, Jeremy Rockliff, said there would be government emergency assistance grants for people on the island who had to relocate due to the fires.

Applications for the grants – which included $250 per adult and $125 per child, with a maximum of $1,000 for any one family – would open from 2pm Thursday, Rockliff said in a social media post.

“For those on the frontline fighting the fire, thank you,” Rockliff said. “We could not be more grateful for your efforts.”

Robert Lawry, a community information officer at the Bureau of Meteorology, said the wind was expected to drop overnight and remain “really quite light” until later on Thursday, which should assist firefighting efforts.

“It’s generally a less windy situation for the next 24 hours,” he said on Wednesday night.

“The humidity will come up through the night as well, and that tends to be a positive for firefighting as well.”

Lawry urged people to check the TasALERT website for the most up to date information and instructions, and to follow authorities’ advice.

A Bureau of Meteorology post on X earlier on Wednesday featured a video showing a vast column of smoke being blown south across north-east Tasmania, as northerly winds pushed the plume across Bass Strait.

Roughly 3,000 hectares had been burned by the fire on Tuesday, before it spread south on Wednesday following a wind change.

Residents on the island, which is about 130,000 hectares in size and home to 900 people, posted photos of massive plumes of smoke on social media.

Mick Grimshaw, a farmer, helped friends move cattle from their property and said they had lost some fences.

“We were under the ashes. Right there. But we’ve got them safe,” he told ABC radio.

“The fire threat for this farm looks like it has abated a bit but certainly not further down the island.

“We can see the smoke front heading right down the guts of the island.”

Nearly 40 firefighters were working to control the bushfire, plus 12 parks and wildlife staff, five helicopters and three aircraft.

“Additional resources are being deployed and Tasmania Police is also helping evacuate people, particularly in the Leeka and Mount Tanner areas,” parks minister Nick Duigan said.

“There is a lot of smoke in the area and it’s now coming down Tasmania’s coast.”

Several roads were closed because of poor visibility due to smoke.

Flinders Island is known for high-quality exports, including beef, lamb, wool and seafood.

australia.title: Confused about who to vote for in the Victoria state election 2026? A guide to key promises and policies from Labor, Coalition, Greens and One Nation
australia.snippet: From cost of living to health, transport and crime, here is a summary of some of the major promises and policies announced by parties ahe...
australia.content:
As Victorians vote in the state election this month, the cost of living, healthcare, housing and more are high on people’s minds.

Labor, the Coalition, the Greens and One Nation all have their ideas on how to tackle a range of pressing issues – so just what exactly are the parties promising to do if they win?

It’s important to note that not all election promises have been costed and some of the cost estimates provided by the parties have not been independently verified.

Here’s what we know about some of the key promises across major policy areas.

world.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
world.snippet: Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park A Swiss touri...
world.content:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

world.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
world.snippet: Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections The UK sent a Sri La...
world.content:
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”

Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.

Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

world.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
world.snippet: Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa When the ...
world.content:
When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.

In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.

The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.

Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.

“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.

Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.

Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.


A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.

“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

world.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
world.snippet: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship Ukraine has confirmed i...
world.content:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”

Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped over for several days, under a cooperation agreement, to refuel and resupply as it escorted Russian cargo ships that could carry military supplies en route to Russia.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.

Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts to use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The confirmation that Ukraine was behind the attacks was condemned by the UN-recognised government in Tripoli. It said Libya rejected ⁠any foreign ⁠military ​operations on its territory or in its waters.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said Ukraine’s strikes in the Mediterranean “were exceptionally brazen and provocative”.

He added: “The question now is how Russia will retaliate,. Perhaps even more pressing is how the [Hafter] family will respond, given how traumatic the scale of the destruction has been for eastern Libyan authorities.”

Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

world.title: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
world.snippet: No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia A Russian warship docked in th...
world.content:
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.

Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.

Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.

Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.

Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.

“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
